attributes.and_the_college: The College of Levels keeps reference brines; the Compact keeps a standard block. They are different instruments, held by different bodies, answering different questions, and they have never been reconciled to each other. A College water-glass can prove water is fresh. It cannot prove what fresh water is worth, and the Compact cannot be made to say.
attributes.date: RR 47, a hundred and fifty-six years before the present. The Salt Assembly was chartered under it in the same year.
attributes.on_ysolys_tally_stick: It is the fifth head of the Compact that makes a yard of notched rim-oak worth as much at a weighbridge as a house ledger. It is also the fifth head that makes it worth as much to the people she owes.
attributes.sealed_at: the Dry Ferry - the only rock on the plain, and the only ground between the rims that belonged to neither of them. It is thirteen days from Bell Harrow and twenty-eight from Tallow Reach, and Tallow Reach has been making that point for a hundred and fifty years.
attributes.sealed_by: the councils of Bell Harrow and Tallow Reach, and eleven salt houses. The Wardenry did not sign; it acceded in RR 48, because its fees are paid in salt and it could not assess them against a measure it did not recognise. It has been quietly resenting the sequence ever since.
attributes.the_standards: The two sealed half-blocks at the rim weighbridges; the moulds at the Bell Harrow kilns; and the ten-pound water weight, a plain iron cylinder the length of a forearm, of which there is one at each weighbridge and a copy in every counting-house, licence office and depot on the Road. It is the most copied object in the world and nobody can name who cast the first one.
attributes.weakness: It fixes the measure and not the price, and there is no appeal from an assay. A master who believes her salt has been under-graded at the far rim may say so; the weighbridge may weigh it again against the same sealed half-block; and that is the entirety of the remedy.
attributes.what_it_does_not_cover: Water. The Compact weighs water to the pound and says nothing whatever about who owns any - that was the Statute's business, and until RR 167 the Statute only reached wells. Fresh water at the centre is therefore a quantity the Compact can weigh exactly and cannot price at all: there is no standard block for it, no sealed reference, and no body chartered to assess it. The first person who tries to put a figure on the Centre will be inventing an instrument, not applying one, and whoever invents it owns the answer.
attributes.what_it_fixes:
(1) THE BLOCK. Salt is pressed to one mould and one weight - forty pounds, the block, first or second grade by assay. All salt within the bounds is reckoned in blocks and in nothing else.

(2) THE POUND AND THE GALLON. A gallon of sweet water weighs ten pounds. This is the sentence the whole Road runs on. It is why water at the Bell Harrow weighbridge is weighed and not measured, why a thirty-gallon butt is a three-hundred-pound butt, and why a master can be held to the Third Article's carry by a scale rather than by anyone's word.

(3) THE HEAD. 'The head', in any instrument within the bounds, means one person named on a licence. The Third Article of RR 1 required two gallons the head the day and never said what a head was; the Compact said it, and the weighbridges have read it that way since. Draught beasts are not heads. They are not in the statutory carry, they are reckoned on the master's own tally, and the law does not look at them.

(4) THE ASSAY. Grade is set against a standard block, cut from one pressing in RR 47 and split - half sealed at the Bell Harrow weighbridge, half at Tallow Reach. Salt is assayed against the nearer half and priced on the assay. The two halves have been brought together and compared four times in two centuries and have never been found to disagree, which everyone says is remarkable and nobody has proposed testing a fifth time.

(5) THE BOOK OF ACCOUNT. A tally cut by the master of a licensed crossing, in the presence of her own hands, is a book of account at any weighbridge within the bounds - as good as a ledger and admissible at either rim. It records what she is owed and, in exactly the same notches, what she owes.

(6) THE ASSESSOR. The price of salt at each rim is assessed at the turn of each season by the body chartered here for the purpose. That body is the Salt Assembly.
attributes.why_it_is_the_second_document: Because the Statute is denominated in it. The Fourth Article pays a finder 'the worth of the ground at the last assessed price of salt' - assessed under the Compact, by the Assembly, on the Assembly's own weighbridge. Licence fees and well-tolls are paid in blocks the Compact defines. Wages, death-shares, ballast shortfalls and forward salt are all figures in a measure one private syndicate assesses. So when the Wardenry seals ground under the Fourth Article, it is not the Wardenry that decides what the Wardenry must pay for it. Nobody designed that. It is what happens when you write the law in RR 1 and the ruler in RR 47.

name: The Compact of Weights
summary: Sealed at the Dry Ferry in RR 47 by the councils of both rim-cities and eleven salt houses, the Compact did the one thing the Roadwarden Statute had not thought to do: it said what a pound and a gallon and a block of salt actually are. It fixed the mould, the assay and the measure; it made a caravan master's tally-stick a book of account at any weighbridge within the bounds; and it handed the assessing of salt to a body it chartered for the purpose, which is the Salt Assembly. The Statute says what may be done on the Meniscus. The Compact says what things weigh, and every figure in the Statute - every fee, toll, wage, death-share and compensation - is denominated in it.
